topics.title: Big-O and Complexity Analysis
topics.interviewDefinition: Big-O describes how runtime or auxiliary memory grows as input size grows; it is an upper-bound tool for comparing scalability, not a wall-clock measurement. In backend work it helps identify hot paths such as nested request processing, unbounded in-memory aggregation, and inefficient lookups. State both time and space complexity and distinguish average from worst case when a data structure has collisions.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is Big-O not enough for a latency decision?
interviewQuestions.answer: It ignores constants, I/O, allocation, contention, and data distribution. Use it to rule out poor growth, then measure the real workload.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the complexity of two nested loops?
interviewQuestions.answer: Usually O(n²) when both ranges scale with n; inspect whether the inner loop is bounded or advances independently before claiming that.

topics.title: Binary Search
topics.interviewDefinition: Binary search finds a target in a sorted search space by comparing with the middle element and discarding half the remaining range. It runs in O(log n) time and the iterative form uses O(1) extra space. The ordering must match the comparison; it is often used over sorted IDs, timestamps, or answer ranges rather than arbitrary unsorted data.

interviewQuestions.question: What prerequisite does binary search have?
interviewQuestions.answer: The search space must be ordered according to the comparison used.

interviewQuestions.question: Why avoid (left + right) / 2?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can overflow for large integer indexes; the difference form avoids that.

topics.title: Sorting Algorithms
topics.interviewDefinition: Sorting arranges values under a comparator. For backend work, know that comparison sorting is generally O(n log n), stable ordering preserves equal-key order, and in-memory sorting should not replace database sorting when the result set is large. Choose a comparator that produces deterministic pagination order.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is stable ordering important for pagination?
interviewQuestions.answer: Without a deterministic tie-breaker, equal sort values can move between pages and cause duplicates or omissions.

interviewQuestions.question: When should sorting happen in the database?
interviewQuestions.answer: When filtering/paging a large dataset; let an indexed query reduce transferred and retained data.

topics.title: Two Pointers
topics.interviewDefinition: Two pointers scan a sequence from two positions, often reducing a quadratic pair search to linear time when ordering or an invariant is available. It is useful for sorted in-memory data and validation logic, but does not make unsorted database data cheap without first ordering it.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the complexity?
interviewQuestions.answer: O(n) after the input is sorted, because each pointer only moves forward or backward.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the common trap?
interviewQuestions.answer: Applying it to unsorted input without accounting for the O(n log n) sorting cost.

topics.title: Sliding Window
topics.interviewDefinition: Sliding window maintains a contiguous range and updates state as its boundaries move. It converts repeated range computation into O(n) work when each item enters and leaves the window once. Use it for in-memory streams such as recent event counts; use time-windowed storage or stream processors for distributed windows.

interviewQuestions.question: When is sliding window applicable?
interviewQuestions.answer: When the problem concerns a contiguous range and its state can be updated incrementally.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes a window invalid?
interviewQuestions.answer: That depends on the invariant, such as duplicate keys, sum threshold, or expired timestamp.

topics.title: Recursion
topics.interviewDefinition: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to smaller instances and relying on a base case. It is natural for trees and divide-and-conquer, but every call consumes stack space and deep input can cause StackOverflowError. Prefer iteration for unbounded request-controlled depth.

interviewQuestions.question: What are the two required parts?
interviewQuestions.answer: A base case that terminates and a recursive step that reduces the problem.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can recursion be risky in services?
interviewQuestions.answer: Deep or malicious input can exhaust the thread stack; validate depth or use an iterative traversal.

topics.title: Dynamic Programming Basics
topics.interviewDefinition: Dynamic programming stores solutions to overlapping subproblems so they are computed once. Identify state, transition, base cases, and evaluation order. It trades memory for time and is useful when repeated calculations make naive recursion exponential.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you recognize DP?
interviewQuestions.answer: Look for optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.

interviewQuestions.question: What is memoization versus tabulation?
interviewQuestions.answer: Memoization is top-down caching; tabulation is bottom-up iteration.

topics.title: Arrays
topics.interviewDefinition: An array stores a fixed-size contiguous sequence, enabling O(1) indexed access. Insertion or deletion in the middle is O(n) because later elements shift. Arrays are useful for compact, predictable in-memory data and primitive-heavy processing.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is array access O(1)?
interviewQuestions.answer: The address is computed from the base address plus index times element size.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the middle-insert cost?
interviewQuestions.answer: O(n), because elements after the position must shift.

topics.title: Linked Lists
topics.interviewDefinition: A linked list stores nodes connected by references. It supports O(1) insertion or removal when the node position is already known, but indexed lookup is O(n) and pointer overhead hurts locality. It is rarely the default choice in backend code compared with ArrayList.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is random access slow?
interviewQuestions.answer: Nodes are not index-addressable; traversal starts at the head.

interviewQuestions.question: When is a linked list useful?
interviewQuestions.answer: When frequent known-position splicing dominates and cache locality is not important.

topics.title: Stacks
topics.interviewDefinition: A stack is LIFO: push and pop operate at one end in O(1). It models nested work such as parsing, undo operations, and depth-first traversal. In Java, prefer ArrayDeque over the legacy Stack class.

interviewQuestions.question: Why ArrayDeque instead of Stack?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stack is a legacy synchronized Vector subclass; ArrayDeque is a better general LIFO implementation.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the complexity of push/pop?
interviewQuestions.answer: Amortized O(1) with an array-backed deque.

topics.title: Queues
topics.interviewDefinition: A queue is FIFO: producers add at the tail and consumers remove from the head. It is fundamental to work scheduling, buffering, and message processing. For concurrent producer-consumer workflows, use a bounded BlockingQueue to apply backpressure.

interviewQuestions.question: Why bound a queue?
interviewQuestions.answer: An unbounded queue can hide overload until memory is exhausted and latency becomes unbounded.

interviewQuestions.question: What does FIFO guarantee?
interviewQuestions.answer: Order of dequeue among accepted items, not necessarily completion order when multiple consumers process work.

topics.title: Hash Tables
topics.interviewDefinition: A hash table maps keys to buckets using a hash function. Average lookup, insert, and delete are O(1), while collisions can degrade performance; implementations resize to maintain a healthy load factor. Backend examples include in-memory deduplication, lookup caches, and grouping request data.

interviewQuestions.question: Why can lookup become O(n)?
interviewQuestions.answer: Many keys can collide into one bucket, forcing a long bucket search.

interviewQuestions.question: What makes a good key?
interviewQuestions.answer: Stable equals/hashCode semantics and a well-distributed hash.

topics.title: Trees
topics.interviewDefinition: A tree models parent-child relationships with one path from the root to each node. It is useful for hierarchical data, but the complexity of operations depends on height: a balanced tree is logarithmic while a skewed tree is linear. Avoid recursive traversal on unbounded depth from external input.

interviewQuestions.question: What determines tree-operation complexity?
interviewQuestions.answer: Tree height; balanced trees are O(log n) for search-like operations.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a skewed tree?
interviewQuestions.answer: A tree whose height approaches n, making it behave like a linked list.

topics.title: Binary Search Trees
topics.interviewDefinition: A BST maintains all left-subtree keys below a node and all right-subtree keys above it. Search and insertion are O(h), which is O(log n) when balanced but O(n) when skewed. Java TreeMap uses a self-balancing red-black tree rather than an unbalanced BST.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is a plain BST not guaranteed O(log n)?
interviewQuestions.answer: Insertion order can produce a skewed tree.

interviewQuestions.question: What Java collection uses a balanced tree?
interviewQuestions.answer: TreeMap and TreeSet use a red-black tree.

topics.title: Tree Traversal
topics.interviewDefinition: Tree traversal visits every node in a defined order. Preorder is useful for copying/serialization, inorder yields sorted keys for a BST, and postorder is useful when children must be processed first. Traversal is O(n) time and O(h) traversal space.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does inorder produce sorted output for a BST?
interviewQuestions.answer: It visits left keys, then the node, then right keys according to the BST invariant.

interviewQuestions.question: What is traversal space?
interviewQuestions.answer: O(h) for recursion stack, where h is tree height.

topics.title: Heaps
topics.interviewDefinition: A heap is a complete tree with a priority invariant: a min-heap exposes the smallest element and a max-heap exposes the largest. Insert and removal are O(log n); peek is O(1). Use a heap for top-K, scheduling, and priority processing, not arbitrary sorted iteration.

interviewQuestions.question: Is a heap fully sorted?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. Only parent-child priority is guaranteed.

interviewQuestions.question: What is PriorityQueue.peek complexity?
interviewQuestions.answer: O(1), while offer and poll are O(log n).

topics.title: BFS and DFS
topics.interviewDefinition: BFS explores level by level with a queue; DFS explores a path deeply with a stack or recursion. Both run in O(V + E) for an adjacency-list graph. BFS finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph, while iterative DFS avoids recursion-depth risk.

interviewQuestions.question: When should you choose BFS?
interviewQuestions.answer: For minimum-hop paths in an unweighted graph or level-order traversal.

interviewQuestions.question: Why track visited nodes?
interviewQuestions.answer: Graphs can contain cycles; without it traversal can repeat indefinitely.

topics.title: Java Architecture: JDK, JRE and JVM
topics.interviewDefinition: The JDK is the development kit containing tools such as javac; the JRE is the runtime libraries and JVM needed to run Java; the JVM executes bytecode. Java source is compiled once to bytecode and each platform's JVM interprets or JIT-compiles it. This separation is why Java is portable at the bytecode level, not because native machine code is shared.

interviewQuestions.answer: The JDK is the development kit containing tools such as javac; the JRE is the runtime libraries and JVM needed to run Java; the JVM executes bytecode

Native libraries and JVM implementations remain platform-specific, so platform independence has boundaries.

topics.title: Class Loading and Class Loaders
topics.interviewDefinition: Class loading finds bytecode, linking verifies and prepares it, and initialization runs static initializers on first active use. The bootstrap, platform, and application loaders delegate parent-first to avoid loading two incompatible definitions of core classes. In containers, class-loader isolation can cause ClassCastException when the same class name is loaded by different loaders.

topics.title: Runtime Data Areas

Stack frames hold local variables and method state, while heap objects are reached through references. This distinction explains why local variables are thread-confined but mutable shared objects need synchronization.

topics.title: Heap, Stack and Metaspace
topics.interviewDefinition: Objects and arrays are allocated on the heap, while each method invocation gets a stack frame containing locals and operand state. Metaspace stores class metadata and grows in native memory rather than the old fixed PermGen area. Heap pressure causes garbage collection or OutOfMemoryError; unbounded recursion consumes stack frames and causes StackOverflowError.

topics.title: Garbage Collection
topics.interviewDefinition: Garbage collection reclaims heap objects that are no longer strongly reachable from GC roots. Modern collectors are generational because most objects die young; collection behavior and pause goals depend on the selected collector. GC does not prevent leaks when a static collection, listener, cache, or ThreadLocal still retains a reference.
